title: Indemnity & professional responsibility
blurb: Why indemnity is a legal and GDC requirement, the types of cover (defence organisation, insurance, employer or NHS), and what accountability means for you.
question: You've just qualified and are starting a job in a mixed NHS and private practice. The practice manager says 'don't worry, you're covered by us'. Later you plan to do some locum shifts and train in fluoride varnish application. What do you need to check about your indemnity, and why does it matter?

teach.body: Indemnity is an arrangement that pays compensation, and usually legal costs, if a patient is harmed by your negligence and makes a claim. Under the Health Care and Associated Professions (Indemnity Arrangements) Order 2014, every GDC registrant must have appropriate indemnity. GDC Standard 1.8 (under Principle 1) says you must have appropriate arrangements in place so patients can seek compensation if they suffer harm. You declare it when you first register and at every annual renewal. Without it, you cannot lawfully practise.

children.label: Defence organisation
children.sub: Membership; discretionary help, advice and support

children.label: Employer or NHS cover
children.sub: Covers work you do for that employer

teach.caption: Dental defence organisations offer membership with discretionary indemnity. Insurers offer policies with contractual cover. NHS trust staff (for example in hospitals) are covered by NHS indemnity schemes run by NHS Resolution.
Claims can arrive years after treatment, so it matters whether cover is based on when the incident happened or when the claim is made.

teach.body: Many employed dental nurses are covered by their employer's indemnity. But don't assume. Ask for confirmation in writing that it covers you and all your duties, including any additional skills such as radiography or fluoride varnish application. Check whether it includes advice and representation if a complaint is made about you to the GDC, which employer cover may not. Locum, agency and self-employed nurses usually need their own arrangement. Many nurses take out their own defence organisation membership as well.

steps.label: Start a job
steps.sub: Confirm who covers you, in writing

steps.label: Change jobs or locum
steps.sub: Arrange cover before your first shift

teach.body: Responsibility is the duty to carry out a task. Accountability is being answerable for your own decisions and actions, and being able to explain and justify them. A dentist can delegate a task to you, but you remain accountable for how you do it, so only accept tasks within your Scope of Practice, training and competence. As a GDC registrant you are personally accountable: 'the dentist told me to' is not a defence.

teach.text: Being employed doesn't automatically mean you are fully covered, and indemnity is not optional. Working without appropriate indemnity breaches the law and GDC requirements, and can lead to fitness to practise action.

items: Indemnity is a legal requirement and a condition of GDC registration.
It lets harmed patients be compensated and supports you if a claim is made.
Types: defence organisation (discretionary), insurance (contractual), employer or NHS cover.
Check employer cover in writing, including extended duties and GDC support.
Accountability means being answerable for your own decisions and actions.

summary: You can now explain why indemnity is a legal and GDC requirement, compare defence organisation membership, insurance and employer or NHS cover, check that your cover matches your role, and explain the difference between responsibility and accountability.

A.q: A dental nurse without indemnity arrangements keeps working chairside. Why is this a problem?
options: Indemnity is optional, though strongly recommended
Only dentists are legally required to hold it
It is a legal and GDC registration requirement
It only matters when treating private patients
A.why: All GDC registrants, including dental nurses, must have appropriate indemnity in place; it is a legal requirement and a condition of registration.

whyNot.0: Indemnity is compulsory for registrants, not just recommended.
whyNot.1: The requirement applies to every registrant, including dental care professionals.
whyNot.3: It applies to all patients, NHS and private.

A.q: A colleague asks what 'accountability' means for a GDC registrant. Which description is most accurate?
options: Being answerable for your own decisions and acts
Passing responsibility to the dentist in charge
Following instructions exactly as given
Keeping accurate accounts of the practice income
A.why: Accountability means you are answerable for your own decisions and actions and can explain and justify them.

whyNot.1: You can't pass on accountability; you stay answerable for what you do.
whyNot.2: Following instructions doesn't remove your accountability if they are unsafe.

A.q: What is the main purpose of indemnity for patients?
options: To pay for their routine NHS treatment costs
To fund investigations into their complaints
To cover the cost of their regular check-ups
To compensate them if harmed by negligence
A.why: Indemnity ensures patients can receive compensation if they are harmed through a professional's negligence.

whyNot.0: NHS treatment is funded by the NHS and patient charges, not indemnity.
whyNot.1: Complaint handling is a practice responsibility, not the purpose of indemnity.
whyNot.2: Check-ups are paid for through NHS charges, private fees or plans.

B.q: A nurse's employer says she is 'covered by the practice'. What should she do?
options: Assume she is covered for everything she does
Ask for written confirmation of what is covered
Cancel any personal membership straight away
Stop doing extended duties just to be safe
B.why: She should confirm in writing that the employer's cover includes her and all her duties, and check whether it includes GDC support.

whyNot.0: Employer cover may not include all duties or GDC representation, so she should check.
whyNot.2: Cancelling personal cover before checking could leave gaps.
whyNot.3: Extended duties are fine if trained and covered; the answer is to check, not stop.

B.q: How does indemnity from a dental defence organisation usually work?
options: It is discretionary, decided case by case
It is a fixed contract with set limits and terms
It is provided free by the GDC
It only covers NHS hospital staff
B.why: Defence organisations provide discretionary indemnity as a benefit of membership, deciding whether to assist case by case, plus advice and support.

whyNot.1: A fixed contract with set terms describes an insurance policy.
whyNot.2: The GDC regulates registrants; it doesn't provide indemnity.
whyNot.3: NHS hospital staff are usually covered by NHS indemnity schemes, not defence organisations.

B.q: When must a dental nurse declare their indemnity arrangements to the GDC?
options: Only once a claim has been made against them
Every five years, at the end of the CPD cycle
At registration and each annual renewal
Only when they change employer or role
B.why: Registrants confirm they have appropriate indemnity when they first register and at every annual renewal.

whyNot.0: Indemnity must be in place and declared before any claim, not afterwards.
whyNot.1: The five-year cycle relates to CPD; indemnity is declared annually.
whyNot.3: Changing employer means checking cover, but declaration happens at registration and renewal.

C.q: A nurse plans to work locum shifts at other practices. What should she arrange?
options: Nothing, as her main job's cover applies
Indemnity that covers her locum work
A letter from her tutor to show each practice
Cover only after her first locum shift
C.why: Employer cover usually applies only to work for that employer, so locum work needs its own appropriate indemnity in place beforehand.

whyNot.0: Her employer's cover is unlikely to extend to work at other practices.
whyNot.2: A tutor's letter doesn't provide indemnity.
whyNot.3: Cover must be in place before she treats any patients.

C.q: A dentist asks you to do a task you haven't been trained for. Who is accountable if you go ahead?
options: Only the dentist who asked
Only the practice owner
No one, if no harm occurs
You remain accountable too
C.why: You are accountable for your own actions. Delegation doesn't remove that, so only accept tasks within your training and scope.

whyNot.0: The dentist is accountable for delegating, but you remain accountable for what you do.
whyNot.1: The owner has responsibilities, but your accountability as a registrant stays with you.
whyNot.2: Accountability doesn't depend on whether harm happens.

C.q: Which statement about indemnity is correct?
options: Employer cover always includes GDC representation
A claim can only be made within a month
Claims can be made years after treatment
Students and qualified nurses need none
C.why: Claims can arise long after treatment, which is why the type and timing of cover matters, including run-off cover where needed.

whyNot.0: Employer cover may not include representation at GDC proceedings, so check.
whyNot.1: Claims are not limited to a month after treatment.
whyNot.3: Qualified registrants must have indemnity, and trainees must be covered too, usually by their employer.

reteach.title: Like car insurance, but for your care
reteach.question: You can't legally drive without insurance, even if you're a careful driver. Why is indemnity similar for a dental nurse?

blocks.h: The law requires it, however careful you are
blocks.body: Careful drivers still have accidents, and the law makes sure the injured person can be compensated. Indemnity works the same way: the law and the GDC require it so patients can be compensated if your care causes harm. Some 'policies' come with the job, like a company car insured by your employer, but you'd still check it covers you and every journey you make. If you drive other cars (locum work) or new routes (extended duties), check again.

explain.body: Every GDC registrant must have appropriate indemnity, by law and as a condition of registration. It is declared at first registration and at each annual renewal.

test.q: Which registrants must have indemnity in place?
options: Dentists only
Dentists and hygienists only
All GDC registrants
Self-employed staff only
test.why: Indemnity is required of every GDC registrant, including dental nurses.

whyNot.0: The requirement covers all registrants, not just dentists.
whyNot.1: Dental nurses and other DCPs are included too.
whyNot.3: Employed registrants also need appropriate cover, often via their employer.

explain.body: Defence organisations offer discretionary indemnity with advice and GDC support. Insurance policies give contractual cover within set terms. Employer or NHS cover protects you for work done for that employer.

test.q: Which type of indemnity is based on a contract with set terms and limits?
options: Defence organisation membership
An insurance policy
Vicarious liability
GDC registration
test.why: Insurance-based indemnity is a contract, with cover defined by the policy's terms and limits.

whyNot.0: Defence organisations usually provide discretionary indemnity.
whyNot.2: Vicarious liability is an employer's liability for employees' work, not a contract you hold.
whyNot.3: Registration requires indemnity but doesn't provide it.

explain.body: Responsibility is the duty to do a task; accountability is being answerable for how and why you did it. Delegated tasks still leave you accountable, so work within your scope, training and competence.

children.edge: Not trained or out of scope
children.label: Say so

test.q: What is the difference between responsibility and accountability?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Accountability can be fully delegated
Responsibility applies only to dentists, not nurses
Accountability means answering for your actions
test.why: Responsibility is having a task to do; accountability is being answerable for your decisions and actions in doing it.

whyNot.0: They are related but different ideas.
whyNot.1: Tasks can be delegated, but accountability for your own actions stays with you.
whyNot.2: Every registrant has responsibilities, including dental nurses.
